text: Anderson Academy. Engineering 509 B: Probability and Statistics. A Foundations course in Anderson Engineering.

Welcome to Anderson Academy. This is Engineering 509 B, Probability and Statistics, the last of the mathematics Foundations courses in Anderson Engineering. It is a Brief course: this overview of about five minutes, then six lectures of about ten minutes each, so about an hour in all. The letter B at the end of the course code stands for Brief. The department code is E N G R, which is spoken as Engineering, so this course is Engineering 509 B.
Questions or feedback are always welcome, by email to garyanderson at mail dot grokbot dot com or on X at garyanderson.

Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty: it describes, with numbers, how likely things are to happen. Statistics runs the other way: it uses data to learn about the processes that produced them. Probability says, given a fair coin, how many heads to expect; statistics asks, given these tosses, whether the coin is fair. Together they are the tools for reasoning carefully when we cannot know everything.

Engineering is full of uncertainty. Material strengths vary from batch to batch. Loads on a bridge vary with traffic and weather. Measurements carry noise. Components fail at unpredictable times. Signals arrive mixed with interference. An engineer who ignores variation designs things that fail; an engineer who understands it designs with sensible margins, tests efficiently, and draws trustworthy conclusions from data.

Here is the map of this course, which follows MIT's eighteen oh five, Introduction to Probability and Statistics. Lecture one introduces probability itself: outcomes, events, the rules of probability, and counting. Lecture two treats conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' theorem. Lecture three introduces discrete random variables, such as the binomial and Poisson, with their expected values and variances.

Lecture four turns to continuous random variables, especially the exponential and the normal distribution, and explains the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Lecture five begins statistics proper: estimating unknown quantities from data, by maximum likelihood and by Bayesian updating, with confidence intervals. Lecture six treats hypothesis testing and p-values, linear regression, and the uses of statistics in engineering quality and reliability.

The prerequisites are Engineering 501 B, Calculus One, for continuous distributions, and helpfully Engineering 508 B, Linear Algebra, for regression. You should be comfortable with fractions, sums, exponentials, and simple integrals. No previous course in probability or statistics is assumed.

Because this is a Brief course, every lecture chooses its examples carefully and leaves out many methods and all the proofs. Probability has a reputation for surprising answers that defeat intuition. The cure is to be careful about exactly what is being asked, to write down the possible outcomes, and to check answers by simple cases or by simulation. A few lines of computer code that repeat a random experiment thousands of times are an excellent check on any calculation.

The backbone of this course is MIT OpenCourseWare eighteen oh five, Introduction to Probability and Statistics, as taught in Spring 2014 by Dr Jeremy Orloff and Dr Jonathan Bloom, published under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike licence. The OpenStax textbook Introductory Statistics and the open textbook OpenIntro Statistics are companions. The wording of this course is original to the Academy.

This course completes the Foundations: two calculus courses, two physics courses, chemistry, biology, differential equations, linear algebra, and now probability and statistics. With them, you are ready for the eight engineering departments of the Engineering library, where probability returns in reliability, signal processing, machine learning, quality control, risk, and experimental design.
Let us begin with the basic question: what does it mean to say that something has a probability?
Lecture 1. Probability and Counting.

Probability starts with an experiment whose outcome is uncertain, such as tossing a coin, rolling a die, or testing a component until it fails. The set of all possible outcomes is the sample space. For one die, the sample space is the numbers one to six. An event is a set of outcomes, such as rolling an even number, which is the set two, four, six. Probability assigns to each event a number between zero and one, measuring how likely it is.

There are two main interpretations of that number. In the frequentist view, the probability of an event is the long-run fraction of times it occurs when the experiment is repeated many times. In the Bayesian view, probability measures a degree of belief, which can be applied even to one-off events, such as whether a particular bridge design will meet its target life. MIT's eighteen oh five teaches both views and uses each where it fits.

Whatever the interpretation, probabilities obey the same rules, set out as axioms by Andrey Kolmogorov in 1933. Every probability lies between zero and one. The probability of the whole sample space is one: something must happen. And if two events cannot both happen, they are called disjoint, or mutually exclusive, and the probability that one or the other happens is the sum of their probabilities.

Several useful rules follow. The probability that an event does not happen, its complement, is one minus the probability that it does. For any two events A and B, the probability of A or B is the probability of A plus the probability of B minus the probability of both, because the overlap would otherwise be counted twice. This is the inclusion-exclusion principle. Diagrams of overlapping circles, called Venn diagrams, make these rules easy to see.

When all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the total number of outcomes. With two fair dice, there are six times six, thirty-six, equally likely ordered outcomes. Six of them give a total of seven: one and six, two and five, and so on. So the probability of rolling seven is six over thirty-six, one sixth, which makes seven the most likely total.

Equally likely problems reduce probability to counting, and counting needs care. The multiplication rule says that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second, independent choice in n ways, the pair can be made in m times n ways. A licence plate with three letters followed by three digits can be made in twenty-six cubed times ten cubed ways, about seventeen and a half million.

A permutation is an ordered arrangement. The number of ways to arrange n different objects in a row is n factorial: n times n minus one times n minus two, and so on down to one. Five books can be arranged on a shelf in five factorial, one hundred and twenty, ways. The number of ways to choose and arrange k objects from n is n factorial divided by n minus k factorial.

A combination is an unordered selection. The number of ways to choose k objects from n, when order does not matter, is n choose k, equal to n factorial divided by k factorial times n minus k factorial. The number of five-card poker hands from a fifty-two card deck is fifty-two choose five, which is two million five hundred and ninety-eight thousand nine hundred and sixty. The question to ask every time is: does order matter?

The birthday problem shows how counting defeats intuition. In a room of twenty-three people, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday? It is easier to compute the complement, that all birthdays differ: three hundred and sixty-five over three hundred and sixty-five, times three hundred and sixty-four over three hundred and sixty-five, and so on for twenty-three people. That product is about zero point four nine three, so the chance of a shared birthday is about fifty point seven per cent, more than half.

The lesson of the birthday problem is that the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people: twenty-three people form two hundred and fifty-three pairs, each with a small chance of matching. Engineers meet the same effect in computing, where it governs the chance of two items receiving the same code in a hash table, and in security, where it sets how long cryptographic hash codes must be to resist collision attacks.

Complements are often the easiest route. The probability of at least one success in several independent tries is one minus the probability of no successes at all. If a component has a one per cent chance of a defect, and a product contains one hundred such components, the probability that at least one is defective is one minus zero point nine nine to the hundredth power, about sixty-three per cent. Small risks add up quickly.

Probability was born from games of chance. In 1654 Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat, in a famous exchange of letters, solved the problem of how to divide the stakes of an interrupted game fairly. Christiaan Huygens published the first book on probability in 1657, and Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi, published in 1713, proved the first version of the law of large numbers, which we meet in lecture four.

Simulation is a powerful companion to calculation. A computer can generate pseudo-random numbers and repeat an experiment thousands or millions of times, estimating a probability as the fraction of trials in which the event occurs. This is the Monte Carlo method, developed by Stanislaw Ulam, John von Neumann, and Nicholas Metropolis in the 1940s for nuclear weapons research at Los Alamos. Engineers now use it to estimate risks that are too complex for formulas.

Many engineering problems involve geometric probability, in which outcomes form a continuous region rather than a list. If a point is chosen uniformly at random in a square, the probability that it falls in a given region is the region's area divided by the square's area. A dart thrown at random at a square containing an inscribed circle lands inside the circle with probability pi over four, a fact that can be used to estimate pi by simulation.

Careful language matters. Phrases such as at least, at most, exactly, and given that change the answer, sometimes dramatically. Before calculating, write the sample space, decide whether outcomes are equally likely, and decide whether order matters. Many famous probability puzzles, and many real-world errors, arise from a misunderstanding of the question rather than a mistake in arithmetic.

To summarise: probability assigns numbers between zero and one to events in a sample space, following Kolmogorov's axioms. Complements and inclusion-exclusion handle not and or. With equally likely outcomes, probability is counting, with the multiplication rule, permutations, and combinations. The birthday problem and the at-least-one rule show how quickly small chances accumulate. Next we ask how probabilities change when we learn something.
Lecture 2. Conditional Probability, Independence, and Bayes' Theorem.

Conditional probability is the probability of an event given that another event is known to have occurred. The probability of A given B is the probability of A and B divided by the probability of B. Knowing B shrinks the sample space to B, and we ask what fraction of it also lies in A. For one die, the probability of a six is one sixth, but the probability of a six given that the roll is even is one third.

Rearranging the definition gives the multiplication rule: the probability of A and B equals the probability of B times the probability of A given B. It lets us compute probabilities of sequences step by step. Drawing two cards without replacement, the probability that both are aces is four over fifty-two times three over fifty-one, about zero point zero zero four five, because after the first ace only three aces remain among fifty-one cards.

Probability trees organise such calculations. Each branch shows a possible outcome at one stage, labelled with its conditional probability given the path so far. The probability of a complete path is the product of the probabilities along it, and the probability of an event is the sum over all paths that lead to it. Trees are the best defence against confusion in multi-stage problems.

The law of total probability splits a probability according to cases. If events B one, B two, and so on are disjoint and cover every possibility, then the probability of A equals the sum of the probability of A given each B i, times the probability of B i. For example, if two machines make sixty and forty per cent of a factory's parts, with defect rates of one and three per cent, the overall defect rate is zero point six times one per cent plus zero point four times three per cent, which is one point eight per cent.

Two events are independent if knowing that one occurred does not change the probability of the other: the probability of A given B equals the probability of A. Equivalently, the probability of both equals the product of their probabilities. Successive tosses of a fair coin are independent; the coin has no memory. Believing that a run of heads makes tails more likely next time is the gambler's fallacy.

Independence is an assumption to be justified, not a default. Two components in the same machine may fail together because they share a cause, such as a power surge, a manufacturing flaw, or a fire. Such common-cause failures are a central concern in reliability engineering for aircraft and nuclear plants. The disjoint events of lecture one are not independent: if they cannot both occur, then knowing one occurred makes the other impossible.

Reliability calculations show independence in use. In a system of components in series, every component must work; with independent components, the reliability is the product of their reliabilities. Ten components each ninety-nine per cent reliable give a series system only about ninety point four per cent reliable. In a parallel, or redundant, system, only one component must work, so the system fails only if all fail. Two independent components each ninety per cent reliable give a parallel system ninety-nine per cent reliable.

Bayes' theorem, from a paper by Thomas Bayes published in 1763, reverses conditional probabilities. It says that the probability of B given A equals the probability of A given B, times the probability of B, divided by the probability of A. The denominator is usually found by the law of total probability. Bayes' theorem tells us how to update a belief about a cause, B, after observing an effect, A.

Medical testing is the classic example. Suppose a disease affects one per cent of a population. A test detects it ninety-nine per cent of the time when it is present, and gives a false positive two per cent of the time when it is absent. If a randomly chosen person tests positive, what is the probability they have the disease? Most people guess about ninety-nine per cent. Bayes' theorem says otherwise.

Work it through for ten thousand people. One hundred have the disease, and ninety-nine of them test positive. Nine thousand nine hundred do not, and two per cent of them, one hundred and ninety-eight, test positive falsely. So of two hundred and ninety-seven positive tests, only ninety-nine are true: the probability of disease given a positive test is ninety-nine over two hundred and ninety-seven, exactly one third. The rare condition means false positives outnumber true ones.

Ignoring the starting probability, called the base rate or prior, is the base-rate fallacy, and it is common among doctors, jurors, and engineers alike. The same reasoning applies to fault detection in machinery, screening for defects, and security alarms: when the thing you are looking for is rare, even an accurate detector produces mostly false alarms. A second, independent test sharply improves the picture, as Bayes' theorem shows when applied again.

In Bayesian language, the probability of the cause before seeing data is the prior, the probability of the data given the cause is the likelihood, and the updated probability after seeing data is the posterior. Bayes' theorem says the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood. Each new piece of evidence turns today's posterior into tomorrow's prior. Lecture five develops this into a method of statistical inference.

The Monty Hall problem is a famous test of conditional reasoning. A prize is behind one of three doors. You choose one; the host, who knows where the prize is, opens another door that has no prize, and offers you a switch. Switching wins with probability two thirds, because your first choice was right only one third of the time, and the host's informed choice transfers the remaining two thirds to the last door. Many trained mathematicians initially refused to believe it.

Conditional probabilities are easy to confuse with their reverses. The probability of a positive test given disease is not the probability of disease given a positive test. In courtrooms, confusing the probability of the evidence given innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence is called the prosecutor's fallacy, and it has contributed to wrongful convictions. Always say clearly which event is given.

Bayesian reasoning has become central to engineering. Spam filters update the probability that an email is spam from the words it contains. Navigation systems combine predictions with noisy sensor readings using the Kalman filter, a Bayesian method developed by Rudolf Kálmán around 1960 and used in the Apollo guidance computer. Search teams have used Bayesian updating to locate lost submarines and aircraft wreckage on the sea floor.

To summarise: conditional probability restricts attention to the cases where the given event occurs. The multiplication rule and probability trees handle sequences, and the law of total probability splits by cases. Independent events multiply, which drives reliability calculations for series and parallel systems. Bayes' theorem reverses conditioning, and base rates matter enormously, as the medical test shows. Next we attach numbers to outcomes with random variables.
Lecture 3. Discrete Random Variables.

A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment: the number of heads in ten tosses, the number of defective parts in a batch, the number of calls arriving in a minute. A discrete random variable takes separate values, usually whole numbers. Its probability mass function lists each possible value with its probability; the probabilities are non-negative and add to one. The cumulative distribution function gives the probability that the variable is at most a given value.

The expected value, or mean, of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of its values: the sum of each value times its probability. For a fair die, it is one plus two plus three plus four plus five plus six, all over six, which is three point five. The expected value need not be a possible value. It is the long-run average over many repetitions, and it is the centre of balance of the distribution.

Expected value is linear: the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, whether or not the variables are independent, and the expected value of a constant times X is that constant times the expected value of X. Linearity makes many problems easy. The expected total of two dice is three point five plus three point five, seven, with no need to list the thirty-six outcomes.

The variance measures spread: it is the expected value of the squared distance from the mean. A useful formula is that the variance equals the expected value of X squared minus the square of the expected value of X. For a fair die, the variance is thirty-five twelfths, about two point nine two. The standard deviation, the square root of the variance, has the same units as X; for the die it is about one point seven one. For independent variables, variances add.

The simplest random variable is the Bernoulli, named after Jacob Bernoulli. It equals one, success, with probability p, and zero, failure, with probability one minus p. Its mean is p and its variance is p times one minus p. Any yes-or-no event, a component passing or failing a test, a bit being received correctly or not, can be described as a Bernoulli variable.

The binomial distribution counts the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability p. The probability of exactly k successes is n choose k, times p to the k, times one minus p to the n minus k. The combination counts the arrangements of the k successes among the n trials, and the powers give the probability of each arrangement. The mean is n p and the variance is n p times one minus p.

As an example, a production line makes parts with a two per cent defect rate, and an inspector samples twenty parts. The number of defectives is binomial with n equals twenty and p equals zero point zero two. The probability of no defectives is zero point nine eight to the twentieth, about sixty-seven per cent; the expected number is twenty times zero point zero two, which is zero point four. Acceptance sampling plans in quality control are built from exactly such calculations.

The geometric distribution counts the number of trials up to and including the first success. The probability that the first success comes on trial k is one minus p to the k minus one, times p. Its mean is one over p: if each attempt succeeds with probability one tenth, you need ten attempts on average. The geometric distribution is memoryless: having failed many times does not change the chance of success on the next trial, which is the gambler's fallacy again from the other side.

The Poisson distribution counts events that occur randomly and independently in time or space at a constant average rate: calls to a help desk, radioactive decays, flaws in a length of cable, vehicles passing a point on a quiet road. If the expected number is lambda, the probability of exactly k events is lambda to the k times e to the minus lambda, divided by k factorial. Its mean and its variance are both equal to lambda.

The Poisson distribution is the limit of the binomial when n is large and p is small, with n p equal to lambda. In 1898 Ladislaus Bortkiewicz famously showed that the number of Prussian cavalry soldiers killed by horse kicks each year in each army corps followed a Poisson distribution. Today it is used to model network traffic, defects in semiconductor wafers, and the arrival of customers in queueing theory.

As a Poisson example, suppose a server receives on average three requests per second. The probability of no requests in a given second is e to the minus three, about five per cent. The probability of exactly three is twenty-seven times e to the minus three over six, about twenty-two per cent. To keep the probability of overload small, an engineer sizes the system for the tail of the distribution, not merely the average.

Two random variables have a joint distribution giving the probability of each pair of values. They are independent if the joint probabilities factor into products. Their covariance measures how they vary together: the expected value of the product of their deviations from their means. A positive covariance means they tend to be large together. The correlation is the covariance divided by the product of the standard deviations, a number between minus one and one.

Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and drownings are positively correlated because both rise in hot weather, not because one causes the other. Correlation also measures only linear association: two variables can be strongly related in a curved way while having correlation near zero. Engineers analysing operating data must be especially careful, because many variables in a plant move together for shared reasons.

The variance of a sum of two variables equals the sum of their variances plus twice their covariance. For independent variables the covariance is zero, so variances simply add. This is why the error in a stack of manufactured parts, whose individual thickness errors are independent, grows only as the square root of the number of parts, not in proportion to it: a fact used in tolerance analysis, where engineers combine part tolerances statistically rather than by worst case.

Expected value also guides decisions under uncertainty. An engineer choosing between designs can compare their expected costs, including the probability-weighted cost of failure. But expected value alone ignores risk: a design with a small chance of catastrophe may have the same expected cost as a safer one. Variance, worst-case analysis, and safety factors complement expected value in responsible engineering decisions.

To summarise: a discrete random variable has a probability mass function. Its expected value is a weighted average, linear in sums; its variance measures spread, and for independent variables variances add. The Bernoulli, binomial, geometric, and Poisson distributions model single trials, counts of successes, waiting times, and random arrivals. Covariance and correlation measure joint variation but not causation. Next we turn to continuous random variables and the normal distribution.
Lecture 4. Continuous Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem.

Many quantities vary continuously: a resistor's resistance, the time until a component fails, the error in a measurement. A continuous random variable is described by a probability density function, f of x. Probabilities are areas under the density curve: the probability that X lies between a and b is the integral of f from a to b. The density is never negative, and its total integral is one. The probability of any single exact value is zero; only intervals have positive probability.

The mean of a continuous random variable is the integral of x times f of x, and its variance is the integral of the squared distance from the mean times f of x. These are the continuous analogues of the sums in lecture three. The cumulative distribution function, F of x, is the probability that X is at most x, the integral of the density up to x, and the density is its derivative, as the fundamental theorem of calculus from Engineering 501 B would suggest.

The uniform distribution on an interval from a to b has a constant density, one over b minus a. Every subinterval of the same length is equally likely. Its mean is the midpoint, a plus b over two, and its variance is b minus a squared, over twelve. Computer random-number generators produce uniform values between zero and one, and other distributions are generated from them by transformations.

The exponential distribution with rate lambda has density lambda e to the minus lambda x for x at least zero. Its mean is one over lambda. It describes the waiting time until the next event in a Poisson process: if requests arrive at three per second, the time between them is exponential with mean one third of a second. In reliability, it models the lifetime of a component that fails at a constant rate; the mean time to failure is one over the failure rate.

Like the geometric distribution, the exponential is memoryless: the probability of surviving another t hours does not depend on how long the component has already lasted. This suits electronic components during their useful life but not parts that wear out, such as bearings and tyres, whose failure rate rises with age. Reliability engineers describe the common pattern of failure rates over a product's life as a bathtub curve: high early failures, a long flat middle, and rising wear-out.

The normal distribution, also called the Gaussian distribution after Carl Friedrich Gauss, is the famous bell curve. It is determined by its mean mu and standard deviation sigma, and its density is proportional to e to the minus x minus mu squared over two sigma squared. It is symmetric about the mean. Measurement errors, heights, manufacturing variations, and many other quantities are approximately normal.

For any normal distribution, about sixty-eight per cent of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, about ninety-five per cent within two, and about ninety-nine point seven per cent within three. This is the sixty-eight, ninety-five, ninety-nine point seven rule. So a normally distributed quantity rarely strays more than three standard deviations from its mean, about three times in a thousand.

To compute normal probabilities, standardise: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. The result, Z equals X minus mu over sigma, has the standard normal distribution, with mean zero and standard deviation one, whose cumulative probabilities are tabulated and built into every statistical package. For example, if a shaft diameter is normal with mean ten millimetres and standard deviation zero point zero two, the probability that it exceeds ten point zero four is the probability that Z exceeds two, about two point three per cent.

Sums of independent normal variables are again normal, with means and variances adding. Scaling a normal variable gives another normal variable. These facts, and the central limit theorem below, make the normal distribution the workhorse of engineering statistics. It is worth noting, however, that real data often have heavier tails than the normal distribution predicts, so extreme events, such as floods or market crashes, may be more likely than a normal model suggests.

Now consider averaging. Take n independent measurements of the same quantity, each with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, and compute their sample mean. Its expected value is mu, and, because variances of independent variables add, its variance is sigma squared over n, so its standard deviation is sigma over the square root of n. This quantity, the standard error, shrinks as more data are collected, but only with the square root: four times as many measurements halve the uncertainty.

The law of large numbers says that as n grows, the sample mean converges to the true mean mu. That is the mathematical justification for the frequency interpretation of probability, and for every engineer's habit of repeating measurements and averaging. Jacob Bernoulli proved the first version of it, for proportions of successes, in his book of 1713.

The central limit theorem says more: the distribution of the sample mean, or of a sum of many independent random variables, approaches a normal distribution as n grows, whatever the shape of the distribution of each variable, provided it has a finite variance. Averages of dice rolls, of uniform errors, or of exponential waiting times all become bell-shaped. Abraham de Moivre found the first case in 1733, and Pierre-Simon Laplace extended it.

The central limit theorem explains why normal distributions are so common: many quantities are the sum of many small, independent influences. A machined dimension is affected by tool wear, temperature, vibration, and material variation; the sum of these is approximately normal. It also justifies the normal approximation to the binomial: the number of successes in many trials is approximately normal with mean n p and variance n p times one minus p.

For example, a fair coin is tossed four hundred times. The number of heads has mean two hundred and standard deviation the square root of four hundred times one half times one half, which is ten. So, by the central limit theorem, the number of heads will be between one hundred and eighty and two hundred and twenty, within two standard deviations, about ninety-five per cent of the time. Two hundred and fifty heads, five standard deviations out, would be overwhelming evidence that the coin is biased.

Quality engineers apply these ideas through process capability. If a dimension must lie within a tolerance band, the fraction of parts outside it depends on how many standard deviations fit between the process mean and each limit. The Six Sigma approach, developed at Motorola in the 1980s, aims for processes so consistent that the tolerance limits lie six standard deviations from the mean; allowing for a conventional drift of one and a half standard deviations, that corresponds to about three point four defects per million.

To summarise: continuous random variables have densities, and probabilities are areas. The uniform, exponential, and normal distributions model equal chances, waiting times and lifetimes, and natural variation. Standardisation turns any normal calculation into the standard normal. The sample mean has standard error sigma over root n; the law of large numbers says it converges to the true mean, and the central limit theorem says it becomes normal. Next we use data to estimate what we do not know.
Lecture 5. Statistical Estimation and Bayesian Inference.

Statistics turns the question around. In probability we know the model and predict the data; in statistics we have the data and want to learn about the model. The quantity we want, such as the mean strength of a batch of steel or the failure rate of a component, is a parameter of an unknown population. We learn about it from a sample, a set of measurements, and we must say not only what we estimate but how uncertain the estimate is.

A point estimate is a single best guess at a parameter. The sample mean, the sum of the measurements divided by their number, estimates the population mean. The sample variance, the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean divided by n minus one, estimates the population variance; dividing by n minus one rather than n corrects a small bias, because deviations from the sample mean are slightly smaller than deviations from the true mean.

Maximum likelihood, developed by Ronald Fisher in the 1910s and 1920s, is a general method for estimating parameters. The likelihood is the probability of the observed data, viewed as a function of the unknown parameter. The maximum likelihood estimate is the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable. In practice we maximise the logarithm of the likelihood, which turns products into sums and is easier to differentiate.

As an example, suppose a coin of unknown bias p lands heads k times in n tosses. The likelihood is p to the k times one minus p to the n minus k. Taking the logarithm, differentiating with respect to p, and setting the result to zero gives p hat equals k over n: the observed proportion of heads. For normal data, the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean is the sample mean. Maximum likelihood often confirms common sense, but it also handles cases where common sense gives no clear answer.

A confidence interval expresses the uncertainty of an estimate as a range. For the mean of normal data with known standard deviation sigma, a ninety-five per cent confidence interval is the sample mean plus or minus one point nine six times sigma over the square root of n. The number one point nine six comes from the standard normal distribution: ninety-five per cent of its probability lies within one point nine six of zero.

The meaning of a confidence interval is subtle. A ninety-five per cent confidence interval is produced by a procedure that, if repeated on many independent samples, would capture the true parameter ninety-five per cent of the time. For any one interval, the parameter either is or is not inside; in the frequentist view, the ninety-five per cent describes the method, not a probability that this particular interval is right. This distinction is a frequent source of confusion.

When sigma is unknown, as it usually is, we replace it by the sample standard deviation, and the factor one point nine six is replaced by a slightly larger number from the t distribution, which accounts for the extra uncertainty of estimating sigma. William Sealy Gosset discovered the t distribution in 1908 while working on small samples at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, and published under the pen name Student, so it is often called Student's t distribution. For large samples, t and normal values nearly agree.

For proportions, such as the fraction of defective parts or of voters supporting a candidate, the estimate is the sample proportion p hat, and its standard error is the square root of p hat times one minus p hat over n. A poll of one thousand people with fifty per cent support has a standard error of about one point six percentage points, so a ninety-five per cent interval is about plus or minus three points: the familiar margin of error.

Bayesian inference takes a different approach. It treats the unknown parameter as uncertain and describes that uncertainty with a probability distribution. Before seeing data, a prior distribution expresses what we believe. After seeing data, Bayes' theorem from lecture two gives the posterior distribution: proportional to the prior times the likelihood. The posterior summarises everything we know about the parameter, combining prior knowledge and data.

Consider estimating a coin's bias with a uniform prior, saying every value of p from zero to one is equally plausible. After observing k heads in n tosses, the posterior density is proportional to p to the k times one minus p to the n minus k. This is a beta distribution. It is centred near k over n and becomes narrower as n grows, so with plenty of data the Bayesian and maximum-likelihood answers agree closely. With little data, the prior matters more.

A Bayesian interval, called a credible interval, is a range containing, say, ninety-five per cent of the posterior probability. Unlike a confidence interval, it does allow the direct statement that, given the data and prior, there is a ninety-five per cent probability that the parameter lies inside. The price is that the answer depends on the prior, which must be chosen and justified. MIT's eighteen oh five teaches both approaches side by side so that students understand the strengths of each.

Priors can encode real engineering knowledge. When testing a new batch of a well-established component, previous batches provide a reasonable prior for the failure rate, so a small test can give a confident answer. When the prior is uncertain, engineers check whether the conclusions change much under different reasonable priors, a step called sensitivity analysis. If they do not, the data are speaking clearly.

Sampling methods determine whether any of this is valid. Estimates are trustworthy only if the sample represents the population. Random sampling, in which every unit has a known chance of selection, protects against bias. A sample of parts taken only at the start of a shift, or a survey answered only by volunteers, may systematically differ from the whole. No amount of mathematical care can rescue a biased sample.

The size of a sample can be planned. Because the standard error shrinks as one over the square root of n, halving the width of a confidence interval needs four times as many measurements. Before an experiment, engineers choose n to reach a required precision at an acceptable cost. Destructive tests, in which the item tested is destroyed, make this planning especially important.

Modern engineering statistics often uses resampling. The bootstrap method, introduced by Bradley Efron in 1979, estimates the uncertainty of almost any statistic by repeatedly resampling the observed data with replacement and recomputing the statistic. It replaces formulas with computation and works for quantities, such as medians or complex model outputs, for which no simple standard-error formula exists.

To summarise: statistics estimates population parameters from samples. Point estimates include the sample mean and variance, and maximum likelihood chooses the parameter that makes the data most probable. Confidence intervals, built from standard errors, describe the reliability of a procedure, with the t distribution for small samples. Bayesian inference updates a prior into a posterior and reports credible intervals. Good sampling is essential to both. Next we test hypotheses and fit models.
Lecture 6. Hypothesis Testing, Regression, and Engineering Statistics.

Hypothesis testing asks whether data provide convincing evidence against a default assumption. The default is the null hypothesis, H nought, such as: the new alloy is no stronger than the old one, or the coin is fair. The alternative hypothesis, H one, is what we suspect instead. We compute a test statistic from the data and ask whether its value would be surprising if the null hypothesis were true.

The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. A small p-value means the data would be unusual under the null hypothesis, which counts as evidence against it. Before the test, we choose a significance level, often five per cent; if the p-value falls below it, we reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise we fail to reject it, which is not the same as proving it true.

Return to the coin tossed four hundred times. Under the null hypothesis of fairness, the number of heads has mean two hundred and standard deviation ten. If we observe two hundred and twenty-five heads, the standardised value is two point five. The probability of a result at least that far from two hundred in either direction is about one point two per cent, the two-sided p-value. At the five per cent level, we would reject fairness.

Tests can go wrong in two ways. A type one error rejects a true null hypothesis: a false alarm. Its probability is the significance level. A type two error fails to reject a false null hypothesis: a missed detection. The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis is the power of the test. Larger samples increase power. In engineering, the relative costs of the two errors should guide the choice of significance level: a missed crack in a turbine blade costs far more than a false alarm.

Common tests share the same logic. The t test compares a sample mean with a specified value, or compares the means of two groups, such as the strengths of two alloys. The chi-squared test, due to Karl Pearson, compares observed counts with the counts expected under a model, testing for example whether defects are evenly spread across shifts. Analysis of variance, developed by Ronald Fisher, compares the means of several groups at once.

Statistical significance is not practical importance. With an enormous sample, a difference in strength of a tenth of a per cent may be statistically significant but irrelevant to design. With a small sample, an important difference may fail to reach significance. Reports should give the estimated size of an effect with a confidence interval, not only a p-value. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued a statement warning against treating p less than zero point zero five as a bright line.

Multiple testing is another trap. If twenty independent tests are run at the five per cent level on data with no real effects, the chance of at least one false alarm is one minus zero point nine five to the twentieth, about sixty-four per cent. Searching through many variables until something is significant, sometimes called p-hacking, produces findings that do not replicate. Corrections such as the Bonferroni method, which divides the significance level by the number of tests, guard against it.

Linear regression models a response variable as a linear function of one or more predictors plus random error: y equals a plus b x plus noise. The best-fitting line, in the least-squares sense, minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances from the data points to the line. This is exactly the least-squares problem of Engineering 508 B, solved by the normal equations, A transpose A times the coefficients equals A transpose times the data.

The slope of the least-squares line equals the covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x, and the line passes through the point of means. The coefficient of determination, R squared, is the fraction of the variance of y explained by the line; for a single predictor it equals the square of the correlation. Confidence intervals and tests for the slope tell whether the apparent relationship could be due to chance.

Regression must be used thoughtfully. Plot the data and the residuals, the differences between observed and fitted values; a pattern in the residuals means the model is missing something, such as curvature. Beware of extrapolating beyond the range of the data. And remember that regression on observational data shows association, not causation; to establish cause, engineers and scientists use designed experiments in which the predictors are deliberately controlled.

The design of experiments, pioneered by Ronald Fisher at the Rothamsted agricultural research station in the 1920s and 1930s, makes data collection efficient and conclusions valid. Its principles are randomisation, which protects against hidden biases; replication, which measures random variation; and blocking, which removes known sources of variation. Factorial designs vary several factors together and reveal interactions that one-factor-at-a-time testing misses.

Statistical process control, developed by Walter Shewhart at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the 1920s, monitors production with control charts. Samples are measured at regular intervals and their means plotted against limits usually set three standard errors above and below the process mean. Points outside the limits, or unusual patterns, signal that something has changed and should be investigated. W. Edwards Deming carried these methods to Japanese industry after the Second World War, with great effect.

Reliability engineering applies probability to failure. The reliability of a component at time t is the probability that it survives to t. Lifetimes are modelled with the exponential distribution for constant failure rates and with the Weibull distribution, introduced by Waloddi Weibull, for failure rates that rise or fall with age. Combined with the series and parallel rules of lecture two, these models predict system reliability and guide maintenance schedules and the use of redundancy.

Probabilistic design is replacing fixed safety factors in many fields. Rather than multiplying a load by a single factor, engineers model the variability of loads and of strengths and choose designs for which the probability of failure is acceptably small. Modern structural codes use partial factors calibrated by such methods, and aerospace and nuclear engineering use probabilistic risk assessment, which combines event trees and fault trees, to estimate the likelihood of rare accidents.

Statistics also underlies machine learning, which fits models with very many parameters to large datasets. The ideas of this course remain essential there: separating training data from test data to detect overfitting, quantifying uncertainty in predictions, understanding the difference between correlation and causation, and checking whether data represent the situations in which a model will be used. An engineer who understands these foundations can judge such systems critically.
